title: Calibrated Ambiguity in Multimodal Language Models: Humans reach for cultural references, while models describe the picture
one_sentence: Dixit offers a method for studying useful ambiguity, with bounded evidence of reduced cultural allusion in model clues.
problem: Can generated clues remain interpretable while allowing multiple plausible readings?
method: 350 English Dixit boards, six open-weight VLMs and two prompts; author-coded rubric validation and model-assisted large-scale scoring.
findings: Under minimal prompting, model clues were generally overspecified and less culturally allusive.
Prompt changes helped some models; near-human rubric performance occurred in some conditions.
real_contribution: Operationalizes ambiguity as a communicative resource rather than only an error.
biggest_weakness: Humans chose their target cards; models did not. Author coders and English allusions limit cultural inference; no live recipient test.
claim_boundary: Does not demonstrate cross-cultural flattening, audience comprehension, or history-dependent social meaning.
why_researcher_should_care: Test when ambiguity is useful for a particular audience; measure interpretation separately from rubric judgments.
evidence_notes: Full HTML audited; no national culture inference.
Proposed embodied transfer is a research opportunity, not a result.

Independent culture audit: decoys were selected in response to human clues; author-coder consistency does not establish cross-group construct validity, and English competence is not a culture-neutral baseline.

program_membership.reason: Relevant expression, pragmatics, grounding, adaptation, evaluation or system evidence
